content.text: By the end of this lesson, you should be able to:
Define a pure substance in chemistry
Explain how to test for purity using melting and boiling points
Define a formulation and give examples
Explain the difference between pure substances and formulations

has a very specific meaning - it refers to a substance that contains only one type of element or compound. This is different from everyday usage where "pure" might mean "natural" or "healthy." Understanding purity is important for quality control and identifying substances.
is a single element or compound, not mixed with any other substance.
Pure sodium chloride (NaCl) - only sodium chloride
"Pure orange juice" is NOT pure in chemistry terms - it's a mixture of water, sugars, vitamins, etc.
Pure substances have specific, fixed melting and boiling points.
A pure substance melts at a specific temperature
A pure substance boils at a specific temperature
If a sample of water melts at -2°C to 0°C, it contains impurities.
Impurities disrupt the regular structure of a substance:
In solids, impurities disrupt the crystal lattice, making it easier to break apart (lower melting point)
In liquids, impurities make it harder for molecules to escape into gas phase (higher boiling point)
is a mixture that has been carefully designed to have specific properties or uses. The components are in specific proportions.
Each component serves a specific purpose
Components are in carefully measured proportions
Holds paint together, helps it stick
Remember that "pure" in chemistry means one substance only
Know that impurities lower melting point and raise boiling point
Be able to identify formulations and explain the purpose of each component
In chemistry, pure means only one substance is present
Thinking impurities raise the melting point
Compounds are chemically bonded; formulations are carefully mixed
Define the term 'pure substance' in chemistry. (2 marks)
A sample of aspirin is tested and found to melt over a range of 128-132°C. The expected melting point of pure aspirin is 136°C.
a) Explain what this result tells you about the sample. (2 marks) b) Explain why the melting point is lower than expected. (2 marks)
Paint is an example of a formulation. State two components found in paint and explain the purpose of each. (4 marks)
Explain why pharmaceutical tablets are formulations rather than pure substances. (3 marks)
A student claims that "pure spring water" from a shop is a pure substance. Explain why this is incorrect in chemical terms. (3 marks)
A single element or compound, not mixed with any other substance
A substance present in a sample that is not the main component
The temperature at which a solid turns to liquid
The temperature at which a liquid turns to gas
A mixture designed for a specific purpose with components in measured proportions
The component in a formulation that performs the main function
A component that holds a formulation together
A pure substance contains only one element or compound
Pure substances have sharp, fixed melting and boiling points
Impurities lower the melting point and raise the boiling point
Impurities cause melting/boiling to occur over a range rather than at a fixed point
A formulation is a mixture designed for a specific purpose
Formulations have multiple components, each with a specific function
Examples of formulations: medicines, paints, fuels, cleaning products, alloys
